newsitem.title: USA: California power pool price plan raises concerns.
newsitem.headline: California power pool price plan raises concerns.

text.p: Analysts in California's utility industry are raising doubts about whether the state's proposed electricity exchange will lower power prices very much, the basic goal behind deregulating the state's electricity sector.

"All (power) suppliers will get the price where supply meets demand," said Nancy Day, vice president of customer services at New Energy Ventures Inc, during a municipal utility conference held near Los Angeles on Friday.
When demand is high the proposed Western Power Exchange (WEPEX), "may result in us paying more than under the existing system," she noted.

Currently, the cost of power is a flow through to bundled rates charged by investor-owned utilities, such as Edison International's Southern California Edison Co, PG&E Corp's Pacific Gas & Electric Co and Enova Corp's San Diego Gas & Electric Co, which are allowed a fixed return by state regulators.

But the California Public Utility Commission (CPUC), in a bid to end utility monopolies and bring down electricity rates, decided to launch WEPEX as part of the state's four-year transition to a deregulated market.
Beginning January, all power sold by the utilities within California must be offered to the exchange, which then matches supply with demand and sets a pool price every half hour.

Moreover, the CPUC has ordered utilities to first offer the exchange power from hydroelectric units (typically the lowest-cost generation) and nuclear plants (typically the highest-cost) before moving on to other resources.

These and other "must run" plants will make up the bulk of the state's power supply, possibly at non-competitive prices, warned David Freeman, trustee of the power exchange and the state's independent system operator.
For the first four years of restructuring, he said "only a sliver" of the state's power will come from lower-cost sources like gas-fired power plants.
But Bill Sessa, a spokesman for PG&E noted, "There is excess generating capacity in the West. Utilities have an incentive to push prices down, rather than up."
"It's going to be a buyer's market," he added.
Others are not so sure.

John Fielder, vice president of regulatory policy at Southern California Edison, also said the power exchange's pool price could exceed the rate cap designed to ensure power to residential and small business consumers is at least 10 percent cheaper than current prices for the next four years.

Robert McCullough at Oregon-based McCullough Research, a consulting firm specializing in power transactions, said administered markets, like those in Britain and Alberta, Canada, have proved to be "very volatile and highly gamed."
"We are recommending our clients to avoid using the California power exchange," he noted.

Smaller California consumers are likely to continue buying power from their current utility at the 10-percent discount rate, but buyers can choose to go outside of the pool, setting up direct contracts with any approved power supplier.
Industry analysts also point out that money the utilities collect as "competitive transition charges" (CTC) will be a factor of the WEPEX power pool price.

These special charges are to be used to help ease the financial strain on utilities as they move from a regulated to a deregulated environment, helping them to recover the cost of power plants and facilities no longer needed or competitive.

In addition to the cost of producing power, high-voltage transmission costs, local distribution costs, a three percent public goods charge, and the competitive transition charges must not - when added together - exceed the rate cap.
If, for example, the exchange price were to exceed the rate cap over a given period, there would be no money left over to fill the CTC coffers.
"The utilities may not recover everything," Day at New Energy Ventures said.
PG&E's Sessa, however, said there will be plenty of room between current rates, even with a 10 percent cut, and actual power prices for utilities to recover stranded costs.
But other utility operating expenses, which were previously recovered under bi-annual rate cases, will have to be managed "more like a traditional business," he noted.
